utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, I understood that you would like to address the Bench before calling your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The position is this: That I'm glad to say the next witness, Mr. Banduka, did arrive here yesterday evening. As I informed the Court at 7.00 yesterday, I went to see him. He had, I'm afraid to say, a number of extra documents in addition to those that he had already supplied to the Defence. Two translators spent the morning, at my request, trying to sort those documents out, translators from the Defence team, I should hastily add, and two extra tabs have been added to the bundle, in addition to those documents that my learned friend Mr. Harmon had some considerable time ago. That's tab 7 and tab 8, which I hope won't cause him any great difficulty. However, there are a number of other documents that are still being reviewed and that I need to make a final decision about. I won't be in a position to do that until one of the breaks at the earliest. Furthermore, Your Honour, the witness brought with him two videos, which he said were about an hour long, of various events in the municipality Hadzici that he's going to give evidence in relation to. Technical staff here have been very helpful and have now put those individuals onto CDs and they, too, are going to be viewed this afternoon. I'm certainly not inviting the Court to -- for an adjournment. Let me start that sentence again. I'm not asking for an adjournment. I wish to commence my examination of the witness now. I'm simply putting the Court and my learned friend on notice, if I could put it like that, that further documents may yet be introduced, videos may yet be introduced, before I finish my examination of this witness. His evidence in chief is going to take some little time, frankly. He has a lot of detail to go into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not knowing exactly what these documents will be, of course, it very much depends if these are maps usually there's no problem. If these are short decisions, we're often able to read them, and then of course we'll hear from the Prosecution where they need to do any further reach on them. But I did understand that it's not a request for postponement. Even without hearing the Prosecution, I can imagine that this is not what makes them happy, to say the least. Perhaps we'll get started and see what comes our way. There is, however, one other matter I'd like to briefly address, that is, the presence of the witness when the Judges enter the Court. I was informed that -- of course I couldn't have any knowledge first-hand, that if the witness is in before the Judges have entered the courtroom, that sometimes there are discussions on the Defence side which could be overheard by the witness. I think it's very efficient to have the witness in, but of course the condition would be that there's not any communication that could be overheard by the witness at this moment. So if the Defence would commit itself to that, then the witness may be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd much rather not commit myself to that, Your Honour. But if Your Honour is making --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have to wait until the Judges are in and then wait until the -- and then wait the witness to be brought in at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was Mr. Tieger's understandable concern, and, frankly, the reason I entirely agree with him is, of course, neither Mr. Tieger nor I understand what is being said. And so we can't tell whether what is audible may in some way affect the witness's testimony, even in some small way. And that's the particular mischief of it, or the particular problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps when I said the condition would be that there's not any communication that could be overheard by the witness at this moment, perhaps it would say everyone is silent until the Judges enter the courtroom. Then we could start right away. And of course if there would be any concern about eye contact or whatever, then we'll hear from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm certainly more than prepared to try to -- could I urge the Court staff to bring the witness in as close to the Judges' arrival as possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik's, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is saying that last-minute communication between him and his counsel is essential. But so long as the witness is brought in, shall we say, no more than a minute before the Judges, then I can't see any objection. But the problem is that on occasions witnesses can be in here for some considerable minutes before the Judges arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For various reasons, the Judges, for technical reasons, sometimes we have to wait, sometimes we are late for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was certainly, with respect, not being critical at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We'll further discuss the matter with the Registry and then see how we resolve the matter, and it's clear -- it's good that you have brought to our attention that sometimes the witnesses is in for a considerable longer time than just 30 seconds and we should take that into account when finding a solution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Banduka, if I'm well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Banduka, I take it. Mr. Banduka, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence, will start the examination. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You come -- your name is Vidomir Banduka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You are from the Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were educated in that municipality up to elementary level and then went to secondary school in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You graduated from law school in Sarajevo and then you had a number of jobs, and eventually ended up working in a construction company called, I think, Ingrap, in Hadzici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. But before Ingrap, I worked in the company Zoi 84, which was the organising committee for the winter Olympics in 1984, 1985, and it was after that that I started working for Ingrap.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were a member of the League of Communists when you were younger?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were, in fact, involved in various youth work throughout the former Yugoslavia, and you were the leader of a --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- youth work called the Slobodan Princip Seljo?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. In 1979, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As we will hear in due course, you joined the SDS in 1990?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were a member of the electoral commission in Hadzici for the November 1990 election?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That obviously prevented you being a candidate in that election.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. It was incompatible for a person to be a candidate on a list and a member of the local electoral commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were also secretary of the SDS Municipal Committee, and that allowed you to follow municipal politics in Hadzici very closely?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the war broke out, you in fact joined the VRS for a number of months?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the Army of Republika Srpska from July to the end of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then you were nominated as president of the Executive Committee of Hadzici, a position that you held until after the war?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. At the Municipal Assembly session of Hadzici, I believe it was on the 26th of December, 1992, that I was elected president of the executive committee of the municipality of Hadzici, and I continued holding this position until I moved -- until we moved out in March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You moved out in March 1996 after the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. As it is well known, the Dayton Accords were signed on the 21st November 1996 and we moved out before the -- by the 6th of March, 1996, or rather, I apologise. The Dayton was signed on the 21st of November, 1995. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And presently, you in fact have a job as an advisor in the ministry of security within the BiH government?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Court can see from documentation that it has in its possession that until the war in Hadzici there were approximately 24.000 people, 63 per cent of whom were Muslims, 26 per cent Serbs, and about 3 per cent Croats. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Prior to the multi-party system, how were jobs divided within the municipality, so far as ethnicity was concerned?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: At the time of the single-party system, there existed the so-called ethnic key, as we used to call it colloquially, which meant that all the institutions had to reflect the make-up of the population, the ethnic make-up of the population in the area, which meant that, depending on the number of -- or the size of the Muslim, Serb, or Croat population, an adequate number of position was assigned to them. This was an inofficial quota system. It wasn't really introduced officially. It was the time when the Communist Party was consulted on all these matters and it was the Communist Party that then solved these matters from within its structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did any particular ethnic group, in reality, hold a disproportionate number of top jobs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: First of all, one needs to explain the situation. The municipality as local government did not have competence over all institutions. It shared its competences with the town itself, because the municipality was part of the town of Sarajevo. Sarajevo consisted of ten municipalities. So there was certain competencies that rested upon the town itself, some on the municipality, and some on the republican level. Now, as for the distribution of power, it depended on an individual's influence, whether he was going to be appointed to a position or not. Based on my experience - I was a long-time youth activist - I can tell you that the major positions were mostly given to the Muslims, or rather, to put it this way, they got the largest piece of the cake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In what way did that manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: It manifested itself as follows: This will perhaps sound as my own assessment; however, the municipal authorities did not consist only of the municipal government and municipal administration, but also through the presence of significant companies in the area, like we had the Coca-Cola factory, we had the wood-processing industry, we had the repairs and maintenance complex, we had two military institutions. So power had to be measured also through the administration of these economic resources. One needed the money. In the communist era, the politics exercised its power through crucial, critical persons who were appointed into the companies that proved to be economically strongest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there any resentment on the part of any ethnic group in relation to the old system?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: You see, by the very logic of things, Serbs who were in the minority always felt not really endangered or vulnerable in social terms, but I will give you the following illustration. The Coca-Cola factory was opened in 1986, and ever since its inception, a Muslim was its manager. There was this Hasan who used to be its manager for a period and then they called it, as a joke, Hasanaginica. So there was always a Muslim who was a manager, like the company for the production of concrete structures. There was also a Muslim. Now, politically speaking, the Municipal Assembly was the place where most of the power was concentrated under that system. As far as I can remember, the president of the committee was always a Muslim. It was only in the period starting from 1984 that two year and then afterwards a one-year term of office, rotating office, was introduced, which meant that one person could only be elected for a one-year term of office and then re-elected once again, rather than before, when, according to the earlier practice, they could have held the position for ten years or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The situation changed in 1990 with the creation of the multi-party system. Which was the first party to be formed in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The first party to be formed in Hadzici was the Party of Political Action, or the SDA, just as was the case on the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where in mid-May the SDA was the first political party to be formed. Therefore, in Hadzici, first the SDA was formed, then the HDZ, and only after these two ethnic parties were formed, the SDS was established too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you attend the founding meeting of the SDA in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, together with several of my colleagues and friends, I attended this meeting, or rather, this rally that was held in a gymnasium, in a sports hall, that was jam-packed with people. All the then leading figures of the SDA attended this rally, such as Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Mr. Cengic, Silajdzic, Mr. Mehmed, and so on and so forth. I remember this particular rally very well. At one point, an acquaintance of mine came to fetch me to the first row, so that I was able to see with my own eyes and participate in this inaugural meeting, in a way, which was characterised by all the usual aspects that one such meeting would entail. It was ethnically coloured, so to speak. There were flags, national costumes. I remember late Izetbegovic, who stated, "We were afraid about Hadzici because they had told us that it was a communist nest. However, this particular meeting proves that we have conquered Hadzici." So this was the atmosphere of this particular rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many people attended the rally?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Close to 4.000 people, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I ask you one thing? The Chamber has heard evidence on, well, a lot of municipalities. How much detail do we need in this respect? It's clear that on the creation of the parties, that usually in the municipalities, sections of that, parties were established, that some big shots, to say it, appeared, that some speeches were made. It also -- I think already we heard 10, 15, or 20 times that it was the SDA that was established first, and only then the HDZ. I wonder whether it would be pivotal for this case whether there were 4.000 people in that hall who listened to it or whether it was big-shot A, B, and C, or C, D, and F which were present. Of course, I'm not saying that it could not be important information, but then it's like in children's magazines, where you get a picture, where you say "find the animals in this picture" or "find the --" It's more or less -- all the remainder seems not to be of great importance. Would there be a possibility to -- perhaps I'm more leading. I'm looking to Mr. Harmon. But if you would have asked, "Is it true that in the sports hall 4.000 people were present and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic?" I can imagine that Mr. Harmon would not be that much disturbed by such leading and it would certainly make progress quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Three short comments, Your Honour. The first was exactly that, if I can lead, it will clearly be much quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Secondly, I'm going to move on so far as this witness is concerned. And thirdly, I'll think about it in future, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For example, if you consider the word -- I can imagine that you say that the type of language used, the word "conquer" is a specific meaning. I'm not stopping you from getting any details that are of relevance, but I'm urging you to especially focus on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think, then, we can deal with it this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the HDZ is concerned, they were mainly in the village or town of Tarcin is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. That was where the Catholic church was, and I think that's where they were concentrated. Most of them lived. But it was far from the rally that the SDA party had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And thereafter, the SDS founding meeting was in front of about a hundred sympathisers. And just dealing with the main players within the municipality, the president of the SDA Municipal Board was a man called Mustafa Halilovic [sic], who later became president of the municipality after the elections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. But his name is not Halilovic. His name is Dzelilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry for interrupting you, but before you proceed, I would like to ask you a question from the witness on one specific point. I would like to know, Witness, before the appearance of this situation of multi-party situation, you gave us to understand very well that there was a Muslim majority, that there were Serbs constituting 26 per cent. We understood that there were inequalities, some abuse of power, or people exceeding their power. So I would like you, rather than keeping to general facts, you try to make me understand exactly what was happening locally. What have you seen yourself? Who could have intervened in such a way that tensions arose? Or, on the contrary, in everyday life, was something going to foreshadow these tensions and that they were going to take place? Do you understand my question, first of all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood your question, but I don't know which period of time you have in mind. Do you have in mind the period before the multi-party elections, therefore, before 1990, or do you have in mind the period actually afterwards, before the outbreak of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood me. It was just before the elections, the multi-party elections, before the establishment of the SDA, just before. What happened? How did people live? Was it possible to say that anybody was abusing his position, that the Muslims were exaggerating on losing their position, or did somebody endeavour to try and keep a balance, maintain a balance? Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've understood. When for some 20 or 30 years you always have a Muslim as president of the committee, then the other ethnic groups feel somehow put into the background. Or another example: Where you always have managers of large companies coming from one ethnicity. I've understood you fully. The ethnic quota system was respected to a certain extent; however, it wasn't the same. The position of a president of a municipality is not the same as the vice-president or the position of the president of the Executive Committee compared to that of the deputy president. The situation was such that the Serbs were given less influential, less attractive positions, because the president of the municipality is a professional who has power in his hands, whereas the deputy works on a voluntary basis, doesn't have any power, and is merely there to satisfy the quota system. Similar problems started emerging in Yugoslavia as early as in the beginning of the 1980s. When I was part of the youth brigade in 1979, there was this feeling of brotherhood and unity. However, when I was doing my military service in 1981, in March, there were the first protests by the ethnic Albanians in Serbia. It was in that period that in the general area of Yugoslavia, some misunderstandings emerged which caused difficulties. It was in its inchoate form at the time. We all know how meaningful a cemetery is to people. In Hadzici, some 50 metres from the Municipal Assembly building, the Serbian Orthodox church was standing, and next to it was the Orthodox cemetery. In 1978 or 1979, someone came up with the idea that the cemetery should be moved out in order for a residential building to be built on its spot. Do you understand what I mean? The Serbs were forbidden from burying their dead on that spot, and they were in fact ordered to relocate the remains of their dear ones to a different site on the outskirts of the town. Can you imagine what it means for a nation which in this way loses its history, its traces, dating back 100 years, as if they could not have come up with a different solution? It was already at that time that the Serbs felt insecure, they felt that they were being pushed into the background, that they were being marginalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The leader of the HDZ was someone called Velimir Maric?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the leader of the SDS was someone called Ratko Radic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Ratko Radic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he in fact died a few years ago?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. He died, and so did his wife. She had cancer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you've told us that you joined the SDS soon after that founding meeting; you got this job on the electoral commission. And perhaps, if you could be given the bundle of exhibits relevant to your evidence, you could turn to tab 1, please. This is a list of candidates from the various parties that participated in that election, which we can see --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- the 1st of November, 1990. The document that you've got in front of you, obviously the original one in B/C/S, where did you obtain that document from? Let me ask that slightly differently. I don't think we're worried about where you obtained it from. What is that document? Is it from some sort of official publication?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document dated the 1st of November. I think the elections were held on the 17th of November. These are the lists of candidates of all the parties participating in the elections in 1990 in Hadzici municipality. This document was published by the Vecernje Novine newspaper. This was the official publication of the city of Sarajevo, and that's where these lists were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that be given a number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, we now know exactly where it was published. Of course, it's not a complete list. It starts halfway - the first part - it seems. I do not mind that much. I don't know what the purpose is of presenting it in evidence. So therefore, you see it starts with the second list of candidates. That's the SDS. Then the third list, SDA. Fourth list, fifth list. For the first list, we have only the last couple -- but I don't know what the purpose is. So I'm not complaining, but since the witness said that this was the complete list of candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, if I may. Thank you for that observation, which is absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Following that election, the results were basically as follows: There were 50 deputies in the Municipal Assembly; 23 of them were won by the SDA, 12 by the SDP, 11 to the SDS, and two small parties had three deputies between them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I think the SDS had 10 and the SDP 11. SDA was the first party; SDP was the second; and the SDS, the third, according to the number of candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about the HDZ? I didn't mention them. Did they win any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. seats?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. The HDZ did not win a single seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the functions of the municipality were divided accordingly. Mr. Jelavic [sic] became the president of the municipality. The president of the Executive Board went to a Mr. Samoukovic from the SDS. The secretary of the Assembly went to a Mr. Muriz from the SDA. And the Executive Board was split three Muslims, three Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Just a correction. It's not Jelavic, but Dzelilovic. We've already mentioned him. In general, there was an agreement at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the party that won would get the post of president of the Assembly, and the second-ranking ethnic group would get the place of the Executive Board. And in this case, it was the SDA and the SDS respectively. Elsewhere, positions were allocated according to the number of seats won in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we could, if need be, go through some of the other positions that were decided at that time. But perhaps more importantly, tell the Chamber, if you would, about the power-sharing agreement that the parties entered into, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I've already said what the general agreement was. I think I mentioned that in the document. Apart from the two leading posts, which we've already mentioned, I think the SDS got the post of secretary for town planning and building construction, and national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. It may be my fault, but I meant power-sharing agreement in terms of actually running the municipality rather than the jobs that were given to individuals. Put another way: Cooperation between the parties immediately after the election in order to secure the smooth running of the municipality. Tell the Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Initially - I remember the Assembly well - I was not a member of the Assembly. I was not elected a member of the Assembly, that is. But the secretaries of the municipal party boards were able to attend the sessions and participate in the work, but they did not have the right to vote. They had no decision-making power. And this was what usually happened. The first constituent session of the Assembly was very difficult. It was immediately evident that it was very difficult to reach solutions. A special issue that arose, I remember well, was that of the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, because certain assemblymen from various parties objected to the candidate. They challenged whether he was qualified. But then this was overcome, and he was appointed. I can conclude, firstly, that in 1991 only six sessions of the Municipal Assembly were held, and each one was more difficult than the last. It became increasingly difficult to reach agreement on every issue that the Assembly debated. I think that the Party of Democratic Action, feeling that it was the winner, wanted to change everything that had been inherited from before. They wanted to replace people, appoint new people everywhere, so that it was very difficult for the Assembly to operate. But until October, I think, 1991, there was some sort of consensus, and those decisions that the Assembly had to make were made, albeit with problems. However, then the problems came to a head and then the assemblymen of the Serb Democratic Party walked out of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've gone a little past where we're at at the moment. I want to ask you about two specific problems, briefly, if you can. First of all, is there any difficulty in relation to the replacement of existing staff in various sectors that the municipality had some control over, for example, education and health?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. That's just what I wanted to say when I said that they wanted to replace people everywhere. The most drastic example was that of schools. There were four schools in Hadzici, three primary schools and one secondary school. Due to circumstances, the Serbs had problems with staffing and we were not in favour of the idea that everything that had been inherited from before should be simply swept away, whereas the Party of Democratic Action had quite a different idea. They even wanted to replace staff in institutions over which the Municipal Assembly had no competence, such as the secondary school, for example, which was founded by the city of Sarajevo, or the health centre, where the Municipal Assembly was not competent but, rather, the city. They insisted on signing an overall agreement, a blanket agreement, where everybody could be replaced whether we liked it or not, and this is where we diverged in our viewpoints. First of all, we did not want to overstep the bounds of our authority; and secondly, we did not wish to replace everybody everywhere, all the staff that were already in place. And that was why we were unable to reach any decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about mobilisation in relation to the Croatian war? How was that dealt with by the parties and the municipality in general?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, you see, the war in Croatia certainly had an influence everywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Hadzici municipality. We bordered on Kiseljak municipality, Kresevo, Busovaca. These were all majority-Croat areas. In my opinion, the war in Croatia introduced disquiet. One of the main stumbling-blocks, apart from the problems I've already mentioned, was also, for the reasons I've mentioned, the fact that there were increased activities regarding mobilising reserve policemen. We who walked out of the assembly demanded that the Assembly be informed by the local police chiefs of the ethnic composition of the police force and the reserve police force. According to our information, the ethnic balance had been altered, or rather, it was in favour of the Muslims by 4 or 5 per cent. And you can imagine the disquiet felt among the Serbs, who were already in the minority, when they saw that the numbers of policemen were increasing and that the number of Muslim policemen was increasing in relation to the number of Serb policemen. We wondered why so many policemen were being mobilised. However, we were not allowed even to put this on the agenda. We wanted to have this information presented and debated; however, we were outvoted. This is another reason why the SDS assemblymen stopped attending the Assembly sessions as of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To make your point, you wrote a letter to various newspapers and so on and so forth, signed by the president of the assemblymen's club of Hadzici and Mr. Stevan Janic, and also by the aforementioned Mr. Radic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 2, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just for my information, the list of candidates, will that get any further attention as it had now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it translated on your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I wonder, what's the use of -- I mean, if we are informed about the outcome and that more posts were given to Muslims or less or et cetera, why we should be confronted with six pages of names, someone has to type them all out, unless there's any specific -- I remember that we had one municipality where you could clearly see that all the HDZ candidates came from a certain village which then, of course, supports the testimony which says that very much -- Muslims, that they were concentrated living in that village, then it's clear. But what role could it play that number 25 on the SDS list was -- I mean, if no further attention is paid to it, then at least, unless you convince me of the opposite, I'd consider it a waste of time translating it, copying it, reading it, and then it's still incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Subject to anything Mr. Krajisnik says -- could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to spend too much time on it, but I'm just surprised by the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik makes a point that may become relevant later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But Your Honour, could I say -- could I just say, I do want to make this observation. I ultimately take absolute responsibility. But in my own defence, this was the very first document that the Defence have submitted to the CLSS. We were so pleased to have a document here in advance, well in advance of a witness attending, that perhaps in our rather -- in our over-enthusiasm, we submitted it. I do apologise. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You kiss your first girlfriend only once. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to turn actually to some guidance from the Chamber. Tab 2 is quite a long document. All of it is to a greater or lesser extent relevant. I appreciate that the Chamber will read this document in due course. For my part, I'm happy to invite the witness to summarise it. But if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that would be a good idea, and we would take our time in the first break to read the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you -- you're familiar with this document, aren't you, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you summarise it, please, to the learned Judges.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, you see, first of all, the document was addressed to the public, and it contains all the objections and everything that had happened in previous sessions, the misunderstandings, the impossibility of reaching agreement, outvoting, marginalising, and so on. Because it was impossible to reach any further agreements at the Assembly, the SDS assemblymen walked out, but the assembly continued sitting, without the SDS assemblymen. The aim of this document was to acquaint the general public with the fact that the conditions in the Assembly were irregular, that the Assembly was working under irregular conditions. And we did not wish our walking out to be understood as objectionism or some other form of political struggle. We simply wanted to inform the general public, and this was the only path open to us, to send a letter to the general public explaining our behaviour and explaining everything that I've already said here. This document sets out all these facts, all this evidence, what we thought, what we feared, our concerns that the Assembly would be transformed into something else. In such difficult times, you can imagine the representatives of a party which has entered a coalition with another party leaving an assembly and their coalition partners disregarding this event. Muslims from other parties had already joined them, and they now had a majority in the Assembly. With only 23 votes, of course, they could not have the majority. This is what we wanted to point out in this letter. We wanted to point out that we had been marginalised and that the other side didn't even care about us any more. That was the essence of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was the letter published in Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I don't remember, because Oslobodjenje was already polarised. It was no longer a publication expressing an editorial policy oriented toward all three constituent nations. It was more in favour of some. I remember that Ekspres Politika in Belgrade published this letter. We wrote Oslobodjenje on more than one occasion, trying to have this letter published, and we even invoked the law on the press. They had to respond to our request. But I'm not sure I'm a hundred per cent confident of this, but I don't think that Oslobodjenje published this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the time of the departure from the Municipal Assembly of the Serbs, did you personally experience any intimidation by politicians from other political parties?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, you see, I have to clarify this. After this Assembly session, when we walked out, another Assembly session was held. In our representatives' club, we agreed, and I have to say that this assembly no longer resembled a real Assembly. So I went there alone once again to put forward our demands and to try and reach some kind of agreement. The atmosphere was extremely unpleasant. I was jeered at. An assemblyman stood up and said, "Go and train Chetniks. You're not going to participate in this assembly any more." I asked the president of the Assembly for protection. However, this turned into a circus, and of course I walked out. This multi-ethnic assembly, I think, never met again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The SDA then set up an organisation called the Defence Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. I link this with the last point I've made. I think that the Assembly no longer met because certain problems arose within the SDP party, which also probably had a majority of Muslims. And I think that they felt it was not in order for the Assembly to continue sitting without the SDS. Circumstances became more and more complex, and I don't know how, but in some informal way they constituted this Defence Council. It was more like a group of citizens. I attended it once. I think the intention was to cover up the gap that had now emerged with the failure of the Assembly to meet. There was some kind of organ that could be pointed at as doing work, although I don't think it was a proper organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What evidence, if any, were the Serbs receiving of the formation of paramilitary groups by the Muslims at this time?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, you see, first of all, as I've already said, there was a drastic increase in the reserve police force numbers. We Serbs became suspicious. You can imagine in such times somebody organising something without you. Of course you couldn't trust it. And then there were rumours going round, openly in town, that there was some sort of patriotic league, Green Berets. In our area, there was a centre, or rather, there was a police academy. It was a school for training policemen, that is. And as there were no Serbs there, it was a walled compound. It used to be a hospital, and some ten years before the war it was transformed into a police school, as I've already said. We received information, and this was common knowledge. People were saying all over town that paramilitary units were being trained there, which were officially neither part of the MUP, the police force, nor the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of the arming of both sides as war approached, what effect was there in the municipality due to its closeness to various barracks and arms depots?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. In the municipality of Hadzici, there were four military facilities, that's to say four barracks. The largest one was in Zunovnica, some two to three kilometres from the centre of town. It was at the foot of Mount Igman, spreading over some 30 hectares. There were many arms depots that were dug in under the ground. Then the Usivak barracks, Rijeka barracks, and then the military academy for cadets in Pazaric. The Zunovnica barracks, as far as I know, had a large amount of arms belonging to Territorial Defence. You know that within the military structure there was Territorial Defence, which was a sort of a secondary military force. As far as I know, based on an order by the Secretariat for National Defence of Yugoslavia, the army was stored there and guarded and protected by the soldiers who were deployed to that particular facility. In fact, all there was to the barracks was the arms depot. In view of the barracks' location and in view of the fact that it was the end of 1991 and early 1992, it was very difficult to maintain this facility, because it was surrounded by a forested area and the mountain. It was quite easy to make a forced entry into the barracks to steal weapons and take them away. As for the other two barracks, the one in Krupska Rijeka, as far as I remember, also had Territorial Defence arms. It was fully surrounded and even attacked on the 12th of May, I believe it was. According to the information obtained subsequently through the Red Cross, when exchanges were made, only 12 soldiers had been guarding the barracks, two of which were killed, and the rest were taken prisoners. And then eventually they were exchanged through the Red Cross. I'm telling you all this because there were various stories circulating in the pre- and post-Dayton period about the Muslims not having had any weapons. The existence of these barracks and the amount of weapons contained therein made it possible for anyone to become very well armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question in relation to that. At Pozaric what type of arms were stored there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you anything specific about the Pozaric barracks. As I've already indicated, this was the military training ground. It was actually the military academy barracks, because I myself, as a recruit, went over there for various drills. It was also enforced encirclement, as far as I know. When the army started retreating from Croatia, an artillery regiment, I believe it was, from Zadar, withdrew to this particular barracks. This was a military formation, with heavy weaponry, and we know what a regiment is. I spoke to a person who was an expert in weapons. When the JNA left the barracks, it is well known that it was on the 18th of May that the army withdrew from Bosnia, and the barracks remained encircled, and the Muslim side subsequently allowed them to leave the area. There were some 300 cadets in the barracks who -- most of whom hailed from Serbia, Yugoslavia, therefore. I believe there were cadets from other countries who were there to undergo training. Therefore, the barracks was evacuated, according to this man who told me so, Vidojevic, Branko. All the manpower was evacuated, but all the heavy weaponry that was stored in the barracks stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Within the confines of the population, at least the Serb population of Hadzici, fear took hold, is that right, towards the end of 1991/1992, and guards and watches were organised all over the place?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. As the situation, generally speaking, on the level of Yugoslavia, became more complex, this was reflected in every single municipality. Everyone was afraid of everyone else. I resided at Hadzici, and my mother had been going to the marketplace in Grbavica, in centre of Sarajevo, for years, selling groceries. At least two times a week, we went to Sarajevo. I remember this one occasion - I can't remember the date - from my own place of residence to this spot in Grbavica, we had to cross some 15 checkpoints, some held by Serbs, some held by Muslims. This was in early 1992, where absolute mistrust prevailed. Nobody trusted anyone, and fear was everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what politically did the Serbs decide to do at this juncture?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: In this period, from the point when the Serbs walked out of the Municipal Assembly, a number of meetings were held and bodies, as I said, this Defence Council, then as Council of Citizens, representatives of various political parties met with the aim of preserving the peace and reaching some agreement. The situation in general dictated our next moves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps I can lead you. The next move was the setting up of your own assembly?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, in connection with the establishment of political parties, the SDS was the last one to be established, and it was done as a response to the developments, out of the need of the people to get organised. Now, the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Committee ceased to function. The Serbs abandoned both the active and the reserve police force. The Muslims had been refusing to respond to JNA call-ups, which included the reserve military forces. General Efendic ordered that the Territorial Defence be mobilised. I believe it was in early April. At the time, we were still a state forming part of Yugoslavia; Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence had not been declared yet. There was this incident where some guests at the wedding at Grbavica were killed. Many Serbs treat this particular incident as marking the start of the war. You had other incidents. In Kupres, in Brod municipality, all these events exacerbated the situation and thus bringing chaos to our own municipality. Since we were unable to get organised, the Serbs themselves spontaneously gathered on this venue on the 18th of April, and proclaimed the Serb municipality, which was more an expression of the wish to show the Serb people that they were not left to their own devices simply because the local government wasn't functioning, and out of the desire to gather, to protect their own interests, and to become a partner to the other side. Because ever since we had walked out of the Assembly, none of these officials felt the need to approach the SDS representatives and tell them: Let's sit at a table and try and find some sort of a solution. This was, therefore, the result of a need of ours to get organised that we established the Serb municipality, in order to discuss all these pressing matters, as partners to the other side, the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've talked about three incidents, Grbavica, Kupres, and the municipality of Brod. Very briefly. Do not go into great detail, but could you please explain and tell us what happened in those three municipalities exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My knowledge is based on what I was able to glean from the press and from what the media reported. I would not wish to go into any details or try to relate these. I only know that blood was shed. There were those who were killed in Kupres, Brod, and Sijekovac. It is only now that the bodies of those who were killed at the time are being found. I believe it was in March 1992 that they were killed. I want to add the following: You have to understand us. Those -- that was the Balkans. Rumours were being spread. Everyone was afraid of everyone else. Stories went around the town, going as far as such absurdities that you would think the aliens are coming to invade the earth. One night I went to the neighbouring village with a commander of the police. I went to this one community centre that was in the centre of the village, where people used to gather. When I entered the building, there were some 30 people or so, all of them wearing reserve police uniforms, armed. I knew the man, he was my neighbour, and I asked him, what were all those armed men doing there? He told me, "This was not on your account. This was because we wanted to protect ourselves from possible attack by someone coming from outside, by some outsiders, be it Serbs or Croats or someone else." So the Serb municipality was merely proclaimed to provide physical protection to ourselves from someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you did not really answer my question. You've talked about three incidents. Could you please relate to us what it is about, you've talked about those three incidents. You talked about a wedding at Grbavica, you've talked about an incident in Kupres and another one in the municipality of Brod. What happened? It's very easy to summarise in three sentences. Could you please do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The incident did not take place at Grbavica. You've misunderstood me. It was before the -- it was in front of the old Orthodox church at Bascarsija, where a man who was carrying a Serb flag, his son had been killed, so he killed some guests at the wedding. Even today there is an inquiry into that event, or rather, this man who was carrying the Serb flag was killed simply because he was a Serb carrying a flag. Whereas Kupres is not in the territory of our municipality. Kupres is in Central Bosnia. Bosanski Brod is another municipality bordering the Sava River. What I wanted to say by mentioning these incidents was that blood had already been shed, people had already been injured or killed, and when you see people getting killed 50 kilometres away from where you are and these horrid events, then of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've talked to us about bloodshed. Was it only Serbian blood or was it also Croatian blood or Muslim blood in that way? Was there -- who was killed exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, the blood was shed on all sides. In Kupres, it was Croats and Serb -- Muslims who were -- or Serbs were fighting. In Brod -- the old Orthodox church in the centre of Sarajevo that I mentioned, that was where the Serb blood was shed only. But of course it always takes two sides to enter into a conflict. I was mentioning this as one factor which contributed to the general disquiet, to the heightening of the tensions, the instilling of fear, all of which urged people to self-organise themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll have a break for half an hour, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, this witness seems to be inclined to tell us long stories. Pages 26 and 27 of the transcript today, on the basis of one or two simple questions, taught us a lot about what army facilities were near to a route, where it was easy to break in and to steal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something, when another group retired and that -- whether there were any cadets, et cetera, et cetera. Finally, whether any arms had ever been stolen there, we still do not know after these two pages. That it was attacked on the 12th of May, we now all know, but attacked by whom is still perfectly unclear, whether this attack was a military attack, because the 12th of May might have been in a period of time where there was no arming to prepare for an armed struggle but might have been already when the arms struggle had started. That all of the weaponry was left after the JNA was -- left on the 18th of May is perfectly clear now, and that they left behind everything, but who took it? And I thought, as a matter of fact, that your question was aiming at finding out about arming of the Muslims. And unfortunately, after two pages of answers and hardly any intervention from your side, we still do not know one single thing about it. So therefore, I'd like you to -- perhaps to focus very much on facts, to the extent possible, and also to take the witness by the hand if he starts dwelling about general matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the past, Your Honour has intervened even when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- I'm examining a witness in chief and asked the witness -- and chided the witness gently and invited them, instructed them, perhaps I should say, to answer the question. I would ask that be done on the next occasion that the witness strays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there's always a dilemma for a Judge, because he might interrupt evidence which the Judge does not understand yet as to be very relevant and to come in the next sentence. You would know better. Certainly I'll assist you if the witness does do the same, but let's say primary responsibility is with you, and I'll certainly assist you whenever that would be needed, and I'll fully support you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I mention one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it would be an idea if everyone had a copy of the map of Hadzici. I think it would be a little bit easier when we come to look at the -- briefly, I hope, some of the military operations that took place there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could bring our exhibits, which gives the maps of all the municipalities of Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honours could, I think that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll certainly try and find it. We'll adjourn until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for the late start. Urgent matters do arise sometimes at the 17th of November, which is the day on which the new term of office starts for new Judges and for re-elected Judges, of course, continues. That took some of my attention, which caused the delay. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. In fact, the time wasn't wasted, and I'm very grateful to my learned friend Mr. Harmon, because, as Your Honour will discover shortly, one of the documents that the witness had brought, the OTP had already prepared a translation of that document, and so that's going to make life very much easier later on. We've been liaising as far as that's concerned. So I'm very grateful to my learned friend and his staff. Could I ask the witness to turn to tab 4. Your Honour, whilst that's being done, let me explain what happened here. Tab 4, the witness did provide in advance of his coming to The Hague. We submitted it to the CLSS, and as the index makes clear, they said it was illegible. To be fair to them, it was. However, when he arrived here yesterday and he and I, with the aid of an interpreter, went through his documents, we found another copy of the same document, which was far more legible. I have little doubt that the CLSS would translate this document when we resubmit it, which is what we will now do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, it's right, isn't it, Mr. Banduka - I'm sure I can lead on this - that what tab 4 is, it's the proclamation to the Serbian people of Hadzici municipality and it explains to them that the situation that they face in the municipality is difficult; it explains why the Municipal Assembly had been established; it describes the president, vice-president, and secretary of the municipality are, and deals with the forming of a Serbian police station, Territorial Defence Staff, commander of that staff, and the reason behind those decisions, a general mobilisation request, and also a call for peace. Is that a fair summary of that document?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there anything -- were you involved in drafting that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was your -- or the aims of those of you who drafted it? What were you hoping to achieve?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: As I said, but first just a sentence about this document. It was drawn up after the 11th of March, when the Assembly of the Serb People was held, which was attended by representatives of different parties and all the different components of the Serbian people. Our aim was, first of all, to have transparency in our work, to inform the people that we had been forced to do what we did, as we say in the introductory part of this document, and that the reason we had done it was to protect the Serb people and to attempt to preserve peace. We therefore wished to inform the public that this was not something done by a small group or just a part of the people, but simply to let the people know that all we wanted was to protect them and to keep the peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you distribute this proclamation?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: We distributed it through people. People came on a daily basis and gathered. It was distributed from hand to hand. This was the most efficient method. For example, a man would take a bunch of documents for his street or his village or his neighbourhood, and then he would disseminate it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the document doesn't bear any particular date. It talks about the establishment of the Assembly being the 11th of April. Do you recall when this document was in fact produced?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Just after the Assembly sitting. I think the sitting was on a Saturday, so this would have been ready on the following Monday, I think. On Sunday, a group met again, and then we constituted an advisory council. We couldn't have a proper organ, in the traditional sense, but we established a body which would analyse the situation, monitor the situation daily, give advice, send messages to the population, and I think this was done two or three days after the assembly. I don't think it was more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so far as the Assembly itself is concerned, the founding session took place in the culture-come-sports centre of Hadzici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Drago Milosevic was elected as speaker?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He, in fact, wasn't a member of the SDS. And Dragan Kapetina --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: He wasn't. Kapetina, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was originally in the SDP, he was elected --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: That's why we tendered tab 1, as far as you can recall, from which it is evident that at this founding Assembly, there were representatives of all political options among the Serbs. Gengo Ratko, the secretary of the Assembly, was also not an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you -- various other appointments were made, including head of the police and the commander?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: An advisory body, known as the Serb Advisory Committee or Council of the Hadzici Municipality was also founded on the 11th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were on that body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this advisory body?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The main purpose of this advisory body was, as I said, that the founding Assembly chose what it chose, but it couldn't meet on a daily basis. It was a large number of people, over a hundred. That's why the advisory body was established, to, in a way, stand in for the Assembly, or as, for example, in peacetime conditions, you have a government at the municipal level or higher which functions in between Assembly sittings. Its role was, as we said in this proclamation, to monitor the situation, to calm down the situation, to continue negotiating with representatives of the other peoples concerning the issues we spoke about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, if you would, please, at tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps before that's done, Your Honour, could I ask for a provisional number to be assigned to tab 4, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D105, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And tab 5, please, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D106, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The position is the same here, Your Honour. The witness has found a slightly better copy. I hope that CLSS now will be able to translate this. Frankly, I can't guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks as if it would be possible to translate, if not all, then most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Banduka, was information that was distributed to Serbian citizens, dated the 27th of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Looking ahead in the document, who is it signed by, please?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The advisory body that we spoke about just now formed a commission which we called the Commission for Information. It was the duty of this commission to disseminate information and to inform the advisory body, and later on the Crisis Staff, when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And again, summarising this document, calling upon people to fulfil their obligations to the municipality by joining the Territorial Defence, saying that regulations similar to those of a state of war should be in place. List of Territorial Defence members needs to be made. Deals with communication matters, but also calls for talks, or at least further talks with the SDA to avoid war, calls for equal treatment, and it also mentions the charity Dobrotvor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And again, what was the purpose and aim in producing this document?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The purpose of this document was to inform the people, to counter disinformation and rumours. The document explains to the people that nothing bad is being done, that we are simply trying to manage the situation; that is, that the advisory body, through this commission, is trying to do that. As for the charity organisation called Dobrotvor it was formed at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina and had branches in other municipalities, because we were already receiving refugees. People were already leaving parts of the municipality, going to stay with relatives and so on, and also, there were areas nearby where there was already war. For example, on the 24th of April, at Ilidza, which is the neighbouring -- one of the neighbouring municipalities - it's only some 20 kilometres away - a conflict broke out there between Serbs and Muslims. On the 24th of April, according to my information, six Serbs were killed in our neighbourhood, so to speak. There was already fighting, or at least there were incidents, whatever you want to call them. And we were trying to, conditionally speaking, at least put the Serbs under some sort of control and prevent them from harming others in any way, to prevent them needlessly causing incidents, and so on. That was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At about this time, a Crisis Staff was formed.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Listen, if you would, to the questions carefully and just answer exactly what I ask you. Firstly, why was a Crisis Staff formed?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Because of necessity, because of fear, the need to protect the people from anything that might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who formed the Crisis Staff? That is, who made the decision that one needed to be formed?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: There was talk of this at this founding Assembly, but at the time we felt it was not yet necessary. Later on, the advisory body made a decision to this effect. Learning from previous experience and the legislation of the former Yugoslavia, there was this idea of a Crisis Staff which could be formed in times of natural disasters or emergency situations. The role of a Crisis Staff was technical, to coordinate, to monitor the situation, to gather information on what was happening, because the joint organs had stopped functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could I just ask for one clarification? You said: "Learning from previous experience." Did you refer to experience of a recent period or from a period further back in history? You don't have to give details, but I'd just like to know whether it was recent experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. This was a term that was commonly used. If there was a crisis situation, such as an earthquake or a flood, or any unforeseen situation, that would be a crisis and there would be a crisis staff to manage it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the previous experience you referred to was, I'd say, constitutional experience or legislative experience, or was it any practical experience you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, both. Most often, there were floods in those areas. If there was a flood in a municipality, a crisis staff would be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when had that happened for the last time, formation of a crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know the precise date, but there were floods almost every autumn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that means that every autumn, a crisis staff was formed. Do I understand you correctly? Approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I won't say every autumn, but if there was a flood, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now better understand your reference to the experience. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many people were on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The first time the Crisis Staff was established, there were about 20, but according to the situation, the numbers varied. Various circumstances influenced this. People would leave, for example. They would move away. Or certain members of the Crisis Staff, when the conflict broke out, remained in Muslim territory and spent the whole war in prison, for example, and then they had to be replaced, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic was the president of the Crisis Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were on it; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And for how long did it operate?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, in late May, at the advisory body, we considered the possibility of constituting those organs in accordance with the decisions of the Assembly and to establish an Executive Board so that the Crisis Staff would no longer be needed. And I think it was up to about the 20th of June, 1992. I think that's how long it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When would you say that the armed conflict began in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The armed conflict began on the 11th of May, 1992 - that's what we say officially - when there was a fierce attack by Muslim forces on the centre of Hadzici, where all the Serbs had remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I simply wanted to know the date that the war started, because I'd like to take you back to the 8th of May. That, in many ways, was the final build-up to the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the 8th of May is a significant day to Serbs; it's part of the St. George's Festival; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what happened on the 8th of May, please, of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The 6th of May is also my feast-day, my family feast-day, and I was celebrating it in the way it's usually done. And on the third day after that, St. Mark's Day - that's the name of the Orthodox holiday - the Serbs visit their family graves. They visit the graves of the dead. That morning, I wasn't there, because it was the third day of my celebration, but my house was close to the cemetery, so all those who went to visit the cemetery would drop in for a cup of coffee or a bite to eat. And on that morning, the Muslims had blocked the entrance to the truck maintenance area. And my sister-in-law had gone to work, and she couldn't get there. She came back. She was turned back. And that's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was simple, what happened on the 8th of May, and you go into a lot of detail on whether your sister-in-law was blocked from -- could you tell us what happened on the 8th of May, and if Mr. Josse would like any further explanation, he'll certainly ask for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of May, the Muslims blocked the entrance to a company employing over a thousand workers. This was the technical and repairs and car maintenance company. So they separated one part of the municipality from the other part. They cut it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there any shooting on that day?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say precisely, because, as I said, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move, then, if we may, to the 11th of May. You were -- a few minutes ago you were about to tell us how, in your view, this conflict actually started.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The conflict started -- well, before that, let me just say that the last few days before the 11th of May, most Muslims left the centre of Hadzici. They concentrated themselves in the areas of Pazaric and Tarcin. On the morning of the 11th of May, they launched an attack on the centre of Hadzici over the Tinovo hill, the village of Kasagici and the barracks that I mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for you to explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I invite Your Honours to take the Hadzici map, if at all possible. But there's at least one copy on the ... It's clear the witness will need one. I'm very grateful to my learned friend and his colleagues. They've got a number of copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Presumably, Mr. Banduka, the yellow area that we see in the map is Hadzici town itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did the Muslims depart to a few days before the 11th of May? Perhaps you could be given the pointer.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: They went off in this direction, Dupovci and further on, towards Tarcin and Pazaric. Some of them left in this direction, Grivici, Vrancici, in the direction of Kiseljak and Lepenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Leaving the map for one moment, when you say "they left," who left? Men, women, children, animals? How did they leave, and who left, exactly?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: As I lived, as I said, in Drozgometva, it was in the direction of the Kiseljak municipality towards Lepenica, and I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Show us where Drozgometva is, please, on the map.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Drozgometva. It's a bit hard to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd certainly agree with that.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: You can't see Drozgometva on the map here. Drozgometva is near Grivici. So you have to follow this blue line, Vrancici is to your left and Bare is to your right, but you cannot see Drozgometva on the map here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've shown us approximately where it is. You were there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you see with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, for the record it now does not appear, the witness pointed at the area which is at the north-western edge of the yellow area, which represents Hadzici. Please proceed. And perhaps you could do a similar thing, because I did not closely follow it, in what direction the Serbs left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Muslims left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Muslims left, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
