utterances.text: Some of them -- he said some of them left in the direction of Grivici and Vrancici and the direction of -- and then I missed -- one word is missing. That was also in north-westerly direction, leaving the Hadzici municipality, near to where a place close to the border is Vrancici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say that Muslims left also in a south-westerly direction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could point at it again in what direction the Muslims left so we'll be able to describe it. If you would point at it again, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I've said, they went into two directions, Dupovci, Grivici, and then onwards. That was the road. And the other direction was from the centre of Hadzici, across Zuto, by Grivici, and they passed through Drozgometva, in a column. This particular direction leads toward Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to summarise: The witness first pointed at a south-western direction following the blue line of the river, up to where it bends to purely west, and then further pointed at -- from the village of Hadzici, in north-westerly direction, Grivici, Vrancici. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were, as you've told us, at home in your village. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I saw entire columns of people, some of them on tractors, others on trucks, with their livestock, with all the belongings they could possibly carry. I went to meet the people and talked to them. The Muslims were leaving, and the Serbs stayed where they were. For instance, I myself had nowhere to go. Where was I supposed to go? I stayed at home. At the end of this movement, on the morning of 11th May, an attack started, from the directions that I mentioned, or rather, if you look at Grivici on the map, behind Grivici there is a hill, Ormanje, and people were able to go across the hill to Tarcin and Pazaric, through forest tracks, into the areas where basically most of them went.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may be obvious, but I think you should tell us. Why is it Muslims left?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: In my opinion, which is based on the events that followed, there was a plan in place, which was to evacuate property, children, women, and the elderly, and to cross over to the territories predominantly inhabited by the Muslims and then launch an attack on Hadzici. That was it. For five or six days we observed these columns of people leaving. Nobody knew why they were leaving. Everybody wondered. Although the situation was quite tense, as we previously indicated. Nevertheless, it seemed odd. Several days later, an attack was launched on the centre of Hadzici, where there were Serbs, because they had nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where was that attack primarily aimed at? Which place within Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: You see, when you look at Hadzici on the map, this was the centre of town itself, which is some three kilometres across, perhaps. So the attack was focussed on the very centre of Hadzici, where there were Serbs. Most of them, actually, stayed there. For instance, if you look at the map -- just a moment, please. There you have Tinovo hill. It was on that hill that the fiercest attack was launched. It was on that very morning that some people were killed over there. Then you have another village. Yes, here it is. Kasatici. All these areas had already been placed under Muslim control, because most of the Muslim population left the centre of Hadzici for these particular areas, which was then followed by the attack that I mentioned a while ago. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how successful was the attack?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: From the Muslim perspective, the attack was not successful, because it was repelled. Although we had some casualties, and according to some information we subsequently obtained, the Muslims had casualties too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, very soon thereafter, a number of Muslims were captured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: You see, previously I spoke about this feeling that prevailed among the people that there was a plan in place. In the centre of Hadzici, most of the population that remained there were Serbs. In several neighbourhoods around this area, there were mostly Muslims. In the course of the clashes on this particular day, in an area called Kovacevici - it was a neighbourhood - fire was opened and there were clashes. I found out later on that there were 12 Muslim soldiers there, all of whom wore black uniforms. Interestingly enough - this is something that fits into what I said earlier - nobody was to be found in this neighbourhood, women or children or anyone else. In fact, we perceived them as a sort of a fifth column. Why? Because I believe that it was all planned, their evacuation, including their movable and immovable properties, in order to then launch an attack on what remained in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness keeps referring to "he heard this" and "he heard that." Perhaps he could identify the sources of his information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, would you specifically ask for that. If the witness says, "I believed it was all prepared," then could you please ask him to find out why he believes that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I had tried to deal with that a bit earlier, but I certainly -- I thought I had adduced that, Your Honour. I mean, it's the inference that the witness draws, he's already said, from what happened at the time, namely, the departure, followed by the attack soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could ask the witness: Is it that it was all planned, did you believe that on the basis of the Muslims leaving in columns, as you said, or is there any other reason why you believed that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was primarily the reason why we felt that this was the case. The thing that you mentioned formerly. I saw for myself the columns moving in the area where I myself lived, and I saw the people in the column, only to see them a couple of days later as part of the attack, as attackers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You now -- so you add now that those who left were now among the attackers. Was there any other reason, or was it on the basis of that that you believed that it was all planned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have an additional question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have shown us where you were [indiscernible]. Could you show us where was -- where your house was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About here. You have Grivici and Vrancici to the left, and this red line is the road to my home. So you wouldn't be able to see my home on this map. It is further away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evening, or the day before the attack, so I'm talking about the 10th of May, so what happened on the 8th of May, on the 9th of May? Did you go to the Hadzici centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As I've said, the 6th of May was my family patron saint's day, and I wasn't moving about those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand. So when did you go to the Hadzici downtown area for the last time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I was over there on the morning of the 6th of May, because we have to have -- we have certain rites that we have to perform on the family patron saint's day. You have to go to the church and carry wheat and stuff like that, and you have people coming over to your house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we talk about weapons, what was the weaponry, what soldiers did you see in the city, who was in the city on the 5th of May, or in the morning of the 6th of May, in terms of military, the weaponry, and the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no army there. You had the reserve police force, and they were the only ones who were carrying arms in the streets. There were then soldiers guarding barracks. But no military was to be found on the street that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. But I would like to ask you the following, then: You said: "On the 10th of May, I saw a column of people, of Muslims, leaving the city of Hadzici." You've told us that those were civilians, but did they carry any weapons at that point when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only those who were members of the Muslim reserve police force who wore blue uniforms, very much like the uniform worn by the regular police force, only in a different shade of blue. There were people moving in vehicles, so it was hard to see whether they had any weapons, although I wouldn't say that I saw any, apart from the weapons carried by those in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So when you say that on the 11th of May an attack was carried out against the centre, the downtown of Hadzici, what did you see, what did you hear, why do you tell us that an attack took place on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 11th of May, an attack took place, which happened not so far from where you lived; correct? So what did you see personally? What did you see, what did you witness, what did you hear on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could hear shooting. I told you that the attack was launched from areas that were mostly wooded, fire was opened on the centre of the town, the outskirts. There was shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry to interrupt, sir, but what did you see, personally? What did you hear yourself, with your own eyes -- what did you see with your own eyes, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was shooting from all directions, from all sides. I said that Hadzici was some three kilometres across. I may have been four and a half kilometres away from the centre. That's where my house was. But one could hear shooting, one could see the smoke, as some of the buildings had already been hit by shells and so on and so forth. In the course of the day, at about 2.00 p.m., from the vantage point of my house, I observed the left side of Hadzici. I climbed up to higher ground, from where I could see with my own eyes that from Tinovo hill, fire was being opened from a wood there. The village was -- of Kasatici was being shelled. You could hear and see shooting going on over there as well. There was this one interesting detail. That day, an aeroplane appeared, and to this day, nobody is sure what this was about, whose plane it was. The plane released two bombs, which landed on a village that was populated by the Serb residents there. And this was something that remained stuck in my memory. This was the first day that I saw people getting killed, shooting everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 12 Muslims who - subsequently discovered - had been murdered were seized at around that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I hope I can lead on this. It is right to -- let me ask you one other question before I begin to lead. When did you learn that a number of Muslims had been seized and killed?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: A young man told me about it. I'm not sure whether it was on the 12th or on the 13th. This young man, who regrettably also got killed on the 3rd of September, told me that the Kovacevics got killed. He used to play football and knew some of these people, so I learnt it first from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you learnt it quite soon thereafter. And until quite recently, it's right to say that you were under the impression that they had all been killed by one individual, in revenge for his brother's death earlier the same day? That's right, isn't it? But you have brought with you to The Hague a newspaper article that we find at tab 7. Firstly, Mr. Banduka, this newspaper article is from a publication which bears what name, please?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Dvevni avaz. This is the newspaper published in the federal Sarajevo. It is the paper that has the highest circulation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see it's dated the 27th of June, 2004. And basically --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- what it says -- or it deals with the exhumation of 12 bodies that were exhumed in Krupac, next to Sarajevo, by the federal commission that deals with this sort of thing. Where is Krupac, please, in relation to Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: It would be easier to explain by drawing upon a map. Anyway, the place is some 20 kilometres away from Hadzici, in the direction of Trnovo, or Foca. On this axis from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine. And it's also right, isn't it, that until you read this article, you thought there were 14 victims of this particular massacre; when you read the article, you discovered that in fact there were 12?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The article goes on to say that a member of the commission that we've just mentioned, a Mr. Koso, said that the truck in which the victims had been brought to their burial and, I think it's assumed, execution place, was burnt, and it wasn't easy to identify bodies. However, they were all civilians from Hadzici. They were arrested, or seized, on the 11th of May, 1992, and then killed. It's thought that they spent the night in the police station in Ilidza. And the next morning they were killed in a track -- in a truck - I beg your pardon- that was the property of KTK Visoko. And we can see in the middle of the article the names of the victims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I suppose that what the article says is true. This is information related by a member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've told us when you learnt of the killing of these individuals, two or three days, if that, after it happened. As far as you know, did it become public knowledge among both Serbs and Muslims then, or did it take a little time for the news to filter through to the general population?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question. Could you repeat it, please. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've told us that fairly soon after these people were killed, you learnt that they had in fact been killed. Did that information become widespread quickly, or did it take a little bit of time for others to learn of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Not right away. Later on, through conversations, the story became known. It was veiled, a bit mysterious, because, for instance, I was told that 14 people were involved, because that was the story that went around. Now the location and the numbers changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Let me deal with this completely differently. I really want you to take us through how the dispute, that's putting it mildly, the war escalated in Hadzici between the Serbs and the Muslims. The point I was coming to was trying to find out the extent to which the knowledge that these people had been killed exacerbated the violence. Bearing that in mind, perhaps you'd tell us how the war escalated after the initial attacks by the Muslims on the Serbs in Hadzici on the 11th of May. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Of course this had an impact, both on the Serbs and the Muslims. This was only the start of the war. When one realised that this was no longer only a political difference of opinions, it became a conflict. You had the attack, which yielded greater tensions, enhanced the fear. The attacks never stopped. They did not stop at this. The attacks did not stop, not even the days that were to follow. Gradually, this line separating the Muslims from the Serbs was created, and it remained in place throughout the war, because the attacks kept continuing from the directions that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Show us, perhaps using the pointer, slowly, as best you can, bearing in mind the map is not that detailed, where the line of separation that you've just talked about was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have a date? Because I know the line, the separation line changed. So if we could have a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That wasn't -- the witness didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the area, and I'm wondering, if you ask him to draw a line, if you can indicate -- if the witness could indicate at what point he's referring when he draws a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I know my learned friend is very well aware of what happened, but I asked the question deliberately simply because that's what the witness said. Perhaps -- Your Honour, perhaps I can deal with it this way, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, you've heard what Mr. Harmon for the Prosecution has just said, and he said that the line did alter at times during the war. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: My comment is that the line did not change except in one part of Mount Igman in 1993. All the lines that were established, you can't say whether they were established on the 9th, 10th, or 11th. I said when the Muslims left, and then on the 11th there was an attack. I showed you where my house was. My house was burnt. We'll probably come to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you. Let's return to what the question was. The question was where the line was. Then the small incident was whether the line ever changed. The witness told us that it changed on Mount Igman in 1993. I take it that his testimony now relates to 1992. So could the witness please indicate where the line was, according to his knowledge, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the only map I've got, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Here you see Mutabdzije then you see Kasatici here, the foot hills of Kasatici, and then it comes down to Dupovci, continuing on in the area of Grivici. Grivici, in the beginning, up to the end of June, I think it was, then it changed. Then around the edges of Vrancici and where I showed you that my village and my house should be. That's, as far as I can tell on this tiny map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I suggest the following, Mr. Josse. First of all, the witness drew with the pointer a line which bends from the east of the village of Hadzici, bends down under it and then goes up again and to the villages he mentioned. If it becomes an important matter, I would suggest that during the next break a copy would be made of the map and that the witness marks it and then that you tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to suggest exactly that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I was speaking before my turn. Perhaps we would have the break now, then, so that you can prepare for that, or would it not be a suitable moment? I can tell you that there is a reason why I'd rather not have the break too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now is fine. Perhaps Your Honour would clearly give that instruction to the witness. I know the Prosecution, as I've already indicated, helpfully have got other copies of this map, which I think the witness can mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He could even do it during the break. Let's take care that we get the right colour, because markings on Defence requests are in black. So if you would be provided with a black pen, could you, on a map, also to be provided to you, during the break, just draw that line as you just indicated that, and then we'll see it after the break. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, did you manage to draw the line on the map? And if it's on the ELMO, we can -- oh, yes. Perhaps we put it on the ELMO for three seconds so that the parties -- or do you need it still, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It can go on the ELMO. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then a provisional number to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D107, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps a number could be assigned to the newspaper article, again provisionally, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The newspaper article dated 27 June 2004 will be D108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you further dealing with newspaper and the map, Mr. Josse? If not, I would have a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not the newspaper article. The map, I'm sure I will deal with. Probably quite a lot more to ask about it over the next minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could I ask the newspaper article to be put on the ELMO for a second. And zoom in on the lower part, the lower part, where it says "Imena ubijenih." I pronounce it wrongly. Lower part. Lower. So move the -- yes. Could I ask the interpreters, because there was in the testimony -- the witness said: I thought about 14 persons. Now from this article I learn that there are 12. And I wondered what the line "Imena ubijenih" means. Perhaps I can ask the interpreters if they can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The names of the killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could the interpreters try to find out whether there are 12 names or whether there are 15 names. I first see what seems to be Remzo (Redzo) Cosic and then from what I understand it's Adil, Dzenad, and Uzeir Kovacevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that makes four. Then we have Almir and Miralem Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 6 -- after Kovacevic, 7; Edin Kovacevic, 8; Zamir i Zijad Kovacevic makes 10; Mladen Soldo, 11; Atif Isic, 12; Ismet Hodzic -- no. Hodzic 13 and Pero Medic. That makes 14. So I do not understand, but perhaps you could clarify the issue, Mr. Josse, how this newspaper article giving 14 names to lead the witness to believe that there were 12. I just have difficulties in understanding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I might say, with respect, very helpful observation from Your Honour, who has obviously looked at the document in a painstaking and, as I've already said, helpful manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A position which is required from lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps I'm showing myself up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Banduka, the learned Judge asked, as I've already said, a very apposite question. I think we can deal with it like this. You had said when you arrived here and indeed in your testimony today that this in fact said there were 12 victims of this massacre. The learned Judge counted 14 names. Why have you made what appears to be a mistake?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I didn't count them. However, at the beginning of the text, you see it says "the federal commission for the search for the missing. Yesterday, at the locality of the quarry in Krupac, near Sarajevo, exhumed 12 bodies" and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interprets note that the text continues and says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I looked at that, of course, before I started counting, and I saw the number 12, which is then followed by a part which says "i tri." And I wondered whether that was supplementary to the 12 bodies. But perhaps the interpreters could read -- translate that first sentence and see whether it really is limited to 12.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it says 12 bodies and 3 bags of human bones which could not be added to any of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So and this, of course, is not without significance that what is presented as facts is not only taken from a newspaper article, although the newspaper article refers to another source on which this witness relied. But it's also an incomplete reading of the newspaper article. So we have then three weaknesses. The first is the imprecise reading, the second is that it's a newspaper article instead of a primary source; the third is that we do not have the originals. I'm not saying that for that reason it's totally -- that it could not be used in whatever way, but this kind of material risks -- at least gives a greater risk of this kind of confusion and imprecision. Therefore, more primary sources would be preferred. But we have now dealt with the matter. I don't think that it's a vital issue on the whole of it, apart from that it sharpens our mind that we have to look very carefully to a secondary or even lower-graded sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in one sense, over the last week and a half, I've been here before, it's slightly a different scenario, but not a million miles removed from this one. This Court has given me personally great leeway in trying to come to terms with the Rules of Evidence here. As the Court is aware, they are considerably more relaxed than what I'm used to. If I am allowing evidence or trying to present to the Court evidence that is simply really not admissible and is too far-fetched, then I will endeavour to take heed of that. I certainly wouldn't be permitted to do this at home. I can tell the Court that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you'll also understand, Mr. Josse, that if we say that the Rules are considerably more relaxed, that's certainly true in terms of formal rules. At the same time, as professional Judges, I hope you'll understand that as far as the substance of the evidence is concerned, we tried not to be in any way even a millimetre more relaxed than any other court would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand, and I'm grateful yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, we can hear you counting to yourself. You're double-checking the names, is that right, or the numbers, perhaps I should say?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. I did point out that when I saw this article, I was confused by what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, no one, I take it, assumes that where you said you thought 14, but the newspaper article tells you 12, that if we see that it's 14 in the newspaper article as well, it would only support the reliability of your initial -- of the number you initially gave to the Court. So don't worry about it. It's more important for us at this moment than it is for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the figure in the 65 ter, to be fair to this witness. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd put back on the ELMO the map that you drew of the battle, or the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This map, now given a provisional exhibit number, as far as you're concerned - and take this quite slowly, because it's important - represents the front line at what period of time?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: This was the front line, as I pointed out, at the very beginning of the war. You can see from the names of the villages, of course, it was difficult to draw a precise line on such a small-scale map. And let's say when the fighting took place, the first fighting that I mentioned, and all the fighting throughout May and June 1992, this was more or less at this demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in summary only, please: The fighting in May and June, give us some idea of the course that it took, how persistent it was. Was it daily? Who was doing what to whom?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. I would first like to say what the most important dates are, and we remember them by our losses. After this attack that I mentioned of the 11th of May, there were no infantry battles until the 24th and 25th of May. There was, however, shelling, artillery duels, so to speak. There was an attack on the 25th, another large-scale attack, especially from the directions I mentioned previously. An attack through Kasatici, Tinovo. These were very fierce attacks, and we had 25 men killed. Then there was an attack, as far as I can recall, on the 6th of June, the 10th of June, the 16th of June. I remember those dates because that was when we had losses. Unfortunately, that's the kind of date a man remembers most easily. We had the most intensive fighting and the fiercest attacks in May and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was the Serb response to those attacks?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what I think, and you can see this by looking at the map and other relevant information. The fighting was such that it was the Muslims who attacked, and we defended ourselves. We began to dig Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. trenches, to build fortifications, dig connecting trenches, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You told us at the start of your evidence that you joined the army. When exactly did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I joined the army in early July, around the 10th of July. But there's a big question here. What does it mean to join the army? It wasn't a traditional sort of army, like the kind you find in textbooks. It was organised people defending their homes and their very lives. All the villages within this line were inhabited mainly by Serbs. The Serb population was concentrated in this area. And if I tell you that the defence line was a hundred metres away from my house, that tells you everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And particularly in May and June that you initially talked about, who was controlling the Serb forces in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already said that. From the 18th to the 20th of May, I think the JNA officially withdrew from all of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So there weren't any in Hadzici. And then, as far as I know, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was established, and I think that by July, the law on defence and the law on the army had been enacted, and of course the army was under military command, the command of the staff. This was the period in which the army was constituted. The people defending themselves were transformed into organised military units. In that period, as far as I can recall, the headquarters of the army command was in Zunovnica, and I think it was a battalion, the unit that was there. I am not really very familiar with military terminology. But it was under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm not quite sure about the explanations which I've been given. That's why I need clarification. During these attacks which took place on the 11th of May or the 25th May or the 6th of May or the 10th of June and the 16th of June, how and by whom are the Serb combatants, who are they until the 16th of June? These units, who composes them? Was it only inhabitants, citizens of the village who had weapons and who were fighting? Is that what we are to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was the local population who lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there were no other combatants? Because we heard that in other parts, in other areas, there were groups which were called paramilitary. There were no paramilitary groups there? Those were only inhabitants, those were only citizens of those villages who took weapons and who defended themselves? That's it? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I don't understand very easily: You say that these combats were extremely fierce, with bombs, and this sounds more like professional combat, professional fighting, with troops, with military troops, rather than civilians who have taken weapons and who are fighting to defend themselves or their homes. Hearing your description of it, and the answers which you have now given, I think there's a sort of discrepancy. Perhaps it's only an impression that I have, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what Your Honour means. What kind of discrepancy? I'm talking about the attackers, not about us who were defending ourselves. I'm talking about the attackers. They shelled Hadzici daily. Your Honour is correct. This couldn't be done by someone who didn't know how to handle a mortar or a gun, but all those people had done military service. Every citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia had to do a year's military service and were trained, either as infantry or artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's quite clear, sir. I hope I'm not making any mistake in interpreting what you've said. On the Muslim side, one had a lot of weaponry, you had guns, possibility of shooting shells, firing shells, and on the other side, there were only civilians who had weapons and who were defending themselves, and this until the 16th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does Your Honour mean by the 16th of June? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that there had been attacks which had been particularly fierce, which had taken place on the 25th of May, the 6th of June, the 10th of June, and the 16th of June. Let's stop at the 16th of June. My question is the following: Was there a difference, a substantial difference, between the weaponry of the Muslims who were attacking and the weaponry which the defenders had at their disposal, that is to say, the citizens of the village of Hadzici? Is my question now clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think so. I can't tell you what kind of weapons the Muslims had up there, but we know more or less what was left in the barracks. I can, however, conclude what they had on the basis of the fact that hundreds of shells landed daily, very destructive ones. As far as I can recall, on the 16th of June, some warehouses were hit. These were actually depots containing old weapons, and one of them exploded. It was almost like an earthquake in Hadzici. This arms depot was hit and exploded. This explosion had to be caused by a highly destructive projectile. It couldn't have been done by a bullet. When you say there's a fierce attack and you know that 25 men were killed in one day, then this is not a caress; it's a fierce attack. When I say "attacks," and to link this up with this line I drew on the map: On the 25th, in Kasatici, Muslim forces penetrated into the village of Kasatici, which was half-and-half, and only four civilians were left there, and everybody was killed and everything was burnt down. In the village of Vrancici also, in this other direction, this was also a mixed village. Only two Serbs were left there, and they were never found. They're missing to this day. I have to tell you that there were constant attacks on this area, where we remained and where we were defending ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. I am happy to see you understood my question. I want to thank you for your answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to take matters up from the point that you've just got to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 16th of June was a particularly unforgettable day for you personally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: In this attack, as my house is at the end of the village of Drozgometva, which had about a hundred houses, all of them Serb houses, and my house was the one before the last. In the attack of that morning, they broke through. No one was killed. People fled if they could. But my house and the houses of my closest relatives, the Banduka family, were all set on fire. The people pulled out. My 70-year-old mother took the livestock and fled. She withdrew, actually, deeper into the village, and the attacks were stopped at a certain line. But the part where the Muslims did break through, everything was torched, and my house is gutted to this day, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll come to that in one moment's time. Where were you when this happened?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: At the time, I was at Tinovo hill, where I drew the line here, because the Muslims had nearly reached the area. This is a hill of some 800 to 900 metres of height, and one could command the view of Hadzici fully. You could almost throw a stone and it would reach the centre of Hadzici. Although we were assigned some different tasks, we went to the area and managed to retrieve it, because had this part been taken, we would not have been able to survive in Hadzici. One would not be able to stay there. One would be within range of a pistol, literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when did you learn of the attack on your home? How long after the event, in other words?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: It was that same evening that we learnt about it, because we consolidated our position on Tinovo hill, which is some five to six kilometres away from my house. The houses were still ablaze, and they were in fact still ablaze the following day. Only later on did we manage to move the line a bit forward to the positions that I indicated previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when did you manage to return to the village to see at close hand the damage that had been done?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Two or three days later. The configuration of the lapped was such that if you were at the top of a hill you could see as far as the other hill. I was able to come a bit closer, thanks to the situation, and then I was able to see for myself what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you have brought to this Court a number of photographs that you took in June of this year, one of your house and four of the village church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. But the church is not in my village; it is rather the church in Pazaric, which is controlled by the Muslims, whereas the photographs of the house do depict my own house in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to the church in a moment. Perhaps I can hand you the house. That's a photograph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've told us you took that in June of this year. And did the house look something like that after the attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With some reflection --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we get rid of that so we can better see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see it well here. The house looked far worse than this. We managed to clear away the rubble. You can see that we have made a concrete slab here. I was trying to reconstruct the house. That's why it is covered in here. But there are some other photographs that show what it actually looked like immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For my purposes, Your Honour, this will suffice. I'd in due course ask that that be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That one photograph will be D109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that copies are still to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive them, then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The originals should be given to the registrar now and marked. And then perhaps under those circumstances, since it is a photograph, would there be a possibility to have the photograph copied, Mr. Registrar, by you, exceptionally? Yes. Then you don't have to care about that, and the chain of custody is guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to all concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is the church --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I know where counsel is going, and if we're going to be displaying a picture of a destroyed church in a village in Muslim-occupied territory, I don't see the relevance of it in this case. We previously discussed tu quoque, and I would invite the Court to invite counsel to identify what the relevance is of photographs of a destroyed church in Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, first of all, I do not know whether Mr. Harmon's assumption is right, that you'd now go to the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is something that is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please respond to his question. He says tu quoque is not a rule that can be applied in international humanitarian law. To make it a bit more easy to you: I can imagine that, whereas we now and then hear from what would seem to be clear violations of international humanitarian law, from the non-Serb side, I mean the witness just testified on something that could be perceived, although we have of course not sufficient details, as attacks on civilian targets, which is also prohibited by international humanitarian law. So sometimes it helps to understand a bit of the background and a bit of the feelings that, well, that the people might have had at that time. If that's the reason why you wanted to show it to us, then I would say that it's your time and I would advise you to pay then proportionate attention to such an issue. If, however, there's anything of tu quoque involved, then of course you should explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness should take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I'll ask him. Do you understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't certain whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can understand. Okay. Then it is not sufficient, Mr. Josse, if he takes his earphone off, because he can hear what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we may have been at cross-purposes there, but let's take no chances. He'll have to leave the courtroom. I thought he didn't understand any English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Might have saved you some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, could I just ask you to leave the courtroom for one or two seconds. We're dealing with a procedural matter, and that should be discussed not in your presence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A similar objection was made by my learned friend Mr. Tieger, when I was examining Mr. Djordjevic, and, broadly speaking, I accepted the objection on that occasion because of the period of time to which the witness was attesting. Again, it was his own personal tragedy that he was dealing with. This, in my submission, is completely different, and my learned friend's objection is fundamentally flawed. Of course we're not advancing the defence that's just been mentioned. Of course we're not. But in terms of the context of what went on in Hadzici, these particular atrocities, as alleged by the witness, are of real importance. In a few moments' time, I'm going to go on and deal with, from our point of view, the not very easy topic of the detention of Muslim civilians in the sports and cultural centre in Hadzici itself, the witness having some knowledge of that. Well, these various events need to be put into very clear context of what was going on around those who were, as alleged by the Prosecution, detaining people, maltreating them, so on and so forth. Not an excuse; of course not. But in terms of context, I contend, I go rather further than the way Your Honour put it, it's actually essential for a clear understanding of the testimony of the -- of this particular witness. And my learned friend's objection is, with respect, fundamentally misconceived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, any further -- we should take care that we do not spend more time on the procedural issue than on hearing a few background facts which create a context, which may make it better understandable how, on the ground, people reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed, Mr. Josse. And my guidance that you pay proportionate time on it is still valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I, before we bring the witness back, since he's out of Court, could we go on to a slightly thorny issue, from my point of view, and that's where I'm going and where we're going time-wise, so far as this witness is concerned. Clearly, I'm not going to finish today. I have -- as a result, I have some further documents to review overnight. Any documents that I might adduce, I have now provided - I think I've already told the Court - to the Prosecution. The Court clearly needs to decide the order of matters tomorrow. Personally, personally, I would rather continue my examination-in-chief of this witness first thing Monday morning. There is this issue of possible video which hasn't yet been seen. I would give myself a time restriction of one further hour after the close of business today. Or, alternatively, Your Honour, perhaps we could use some of the time tomorrow and the Court might leave me in a position to finish my examination-in-chief on Monday. I'd be quite content to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, any response to -- or any suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have not seen the video, Your Honour. I don't have a copy of the video. So I don't know if it's going to be used, what is in it, and what is relevant. I don't know when I can expect to receive a copy of that video. We had planned originally to have Mr. Kasagic continue his examination tomorrow and conclude his examination tomorrow, but we're obviously going over. My preference is to finish with this witness on his direct examination tomorrow and then start with Mr. Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since the examination-in-chief of Mr. Kasagic took approximately, well, two and three-quarters of an hour, some of the time was taken by the Judges, it might even -- I mean, it depends on how much time we'd need, Mr. Josse, for the further examination-in-chief of Mr. Banduka. It's already very unfortunate that we have to split up examination-in-chief and cross-examination. If we would cut halfway the examination-in-chief, that would be even more unfortunate, I would say. So let's see if the Prosecution could finish the cross-examination of Mr. Kasagic the second half of the morning. And if you would take some time in the first part of the morning, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My difficulty, Your Honour, is we're going to finish at 7.00. I'm going to have to resume at 9.00. I've already described some of the tasks that I have to do. The video will not be in a position for presentation at 9.00 tomorrow morning. That's the first point. The second point is this: In my submission, it would be desirable to get Mr. Kasagic out of the way, and then really review how much time we have remaining, both on Friday and Monday, to deal with Mr. Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, one of the things, if you look at the video this evening, you might make up your mind as to whether it's really something that could be -- also could be considered as a contextual exhibit. Sometimes these individual videos show a lot of relatively -- matters that are only of relative importance. Of course, I do not know what it is, but to wait and have it all copied if it would not assist much. Of course, but I've got no idea. I'd suggest that we prepare for all solutions, and as soon as you know anything more to give notice, in a way -- of course, I prefer not -- to spend my evenings quietly, but I'd rather get a short telephone call and to know what we're about to do tomorrow. And perhaps Mr. Harmon would be in a similar position, that he'd prefer to get the information once you've worked on it for a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm shaking my head, because Your Honour, with respect, needs to make a decision this evening. If Your Honour says I need to continue at 9.00 tomorrow, that's what I'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't take a decision, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make one other observation, and that's this: If the Court says I need to continue with this examination in the morning, could the Court ensure that I have to finish so that Mr. Kasagic is finished tomorrow. Because I can see the scenario that the Prosecution will then say they need more time for Mr. Kasagic, and that wouldn't be fair on him. They're ready to cross-examine him. In my submission, that's what should happen first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication of how much time you'd need for Mr. Kasagic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to be doing the cross-examination, but I have spoken with Mr. Tieger, and Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will need more time than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He's going to need more time than usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was indicated before. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, weighing several interests, that is, finishing the cross-examination of Mr. Kasagic, and what the result would be if we would continue tomorrow morning with Mr. Banduka, the Chamber would prefer to interrupt the examination-in-chief, start the cross-examination of Mr. Kasagic, as scheduled, tomorrow, and hopefully finish. I see Mr. Tieger comes in, and I don't know whether he considers it to be the good or the bad news.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had an opportunity to look quickly at the transcript, the exchange that took place, while I was on my way down. I simply wanted to ensure that the information that Mr. Harmon provided to the Court as I was en route was going to be provided, and I see my trip was unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm glad my colleague anticipated me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, some messages were received by the Chamber that the 60 per cent guidance that the OTP might prefer to spend a bit more time on Mr. Kasagic and perhaps save that at another moment. The examination-in-chief, apart from the questions of the Judges, took approximately two and three-quarters of an hour. If you take more than the 60 per cent, would there be any chance that you would not finish by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, it's certainly been my intention to complete the examination tomorrow. When you say "any chance," the effort to do so involves, in part, identifying more expedient methods of presenting evidence and showing evidence to the witness. I'm trying to do so. I think I'll have good cooperation from my learned friends on the Defence. And with that in mind, I certainly hope to achieve that. I wouldn't -- that was the reason, by the way, for agreeing that the order of cross-examination would be reversed, because the Court did point out that it would be preferable to permit Mr. Kasagic to leave by the end of the weekend. So I had that in mind and I'm still trying. But I -- there's a lot of material and I'm still working on it in the manner I just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll start tomorrow morning with the cross-examination of Mr. Kasagic, and in the expectation that it will be finished. And as soon as anyone has reasons to believe that this expectation would not be fulfilled, then the Chamber would like to be informed, not at the moment that we are there, but at the earliest moment possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When should the victims and witness service bring Mr. Banduka to this Court tomorrow, if at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understand from Mr. Tieger, it would only be for a very limited moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we say that the Victims and Witnesses Section should organise in such a way that Mr. Banduka is standby and that they receive a message not later than by 11.00 whether there's any chance that Mr. Banduka should appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's clear, then -- we've got only seven minutes left, but let's use our time as good as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll deal with these photographs, if I may, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the proportionate time is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, Mr. Josse will continue cross-examination. We also discussed another procedural matter, that is, when the examination will continue. There is a chance that you'll be further examined in chief by Mr. Josse in the second part of tomorrow morning, but we'll ask the Victims and Witnesses Section to keep you standby but not later than by 11.00 they'll be informed whether there's a chance at all whether we'll continue tomorrow morning. If not, then it will be at the beginning of next week. Please continue, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look at the photographs that we were talking about a short while ago. Listen carefully to my questions, because I think we can deal with this shortly. Where does that church stand? In which village?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Pazaric. To be precise, the village of Osenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And really, we should look at the map as well, unfortunately, because -- it better be put on the ELMO, please. Point it out, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Kazina Bara is the exact name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please mark that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you mark that spot with the black pen.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, as I say, just answer the questions I ask you. When was that church damaged?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: To my knowledge, in the summer of 1992, this was Muslim-controlled territory, so I can't give you the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And your knowledge comes from what source, please?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: You see, throughout the war, people somehow left the area across Kiseljak, and we received the information as early as in the month of August from people who were either exchanged or had somehow managed to keep in touch with the people in Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when was the last time before the war you had visited that church?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The last time I was there was, I believe, in the spring of 1992. I think that it was on the occasion of our Orthodox holiday, Easter, sometime in early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And was the church damaged at that time?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. No. Or rather, at the time, the service was normally held there, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you took those photographs this summer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one other question. When was the first time after or during the war you returned to the village and saw the church in its damaged state?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: When I took the photograph. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honour would like -- perhaps the four photographs could quickly be put on the ELMO, one after the other. I suspect we can deal with them very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's obviously the exterior of the church; is that right, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be marked A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We perhaps -- could we deal with all the photographs under one number and call them the home, A, and then the first picture of the church B, and then C, D, and E?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have then, we have finally five.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that the interior of the church?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next one, please. Another view of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. This is from the outside. It is the other entrance. The church had two entrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the last photograph. That's it. Thank you. And are you able to say, from what you saw, how the damage had been caused?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I saw -- on the basis of what I saw, I realised that it must have been set on fire, but there were also some other elements there. Here you can see on this photograph that there was appended, or rather, adjoining this church, a building occupied by the priest. I found the house now occupied by the Roma people and the backyard is full of agricultural machinery, livestock, dogs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've no other questions on this particular topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for the day. Mr. Banduka, as I just told you, you're invited to remain standby. We do not know whether we'll see you tomorrow or whether it will be at the beginning of next week. If you would please follow the guidance of the Victims and Witnesses Section. I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone or communicate in whatever way about the testimony you have given until now or you still are about to give, either tomorrow or next week. Do you understand that? Then we will adjourn until tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of November 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
